title: Demographic change is coming to South Asia’s classrooms. Will education systems be ready?
gist: South Asia's under-15 population is projected to fall 16% by 2050 (420m to 352m), which could free ~0.5pp of GDP each for primary and secondary education, but only if governments consolidate school systems before fixed costs lock in inefficiency as happened in Europe and Central Asia.

insights.claim: South Asia's under-15 population is projected to decline about 16 percent by 2050, from 420 million in 2024 to 352 million.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Peak youth cohort is passing; long-run demand for K-12 capacity in the region will contract.
insights.locator: South Asia is approaching a new demographic phase

insights.claim: South Asia currently has the second-largest population of children under 15 in the world after Sub-Saharan Africa.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Context for education and consumer demand sizing.
insights.locator: South Asia is approaching a new demographic phase

insights.claim: In Bangladesh and India, more than half of children at the end of primary school are in learning poverty, unable to read and understand a simple age-appropriate text.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Human-capital deficits constrain long-run productivity; remedial edtech has a large addressable market.
insights.locator: Yet access is only part of the story

insights.claim: South Asian countries spend about 3.7 percent of GDP on education on average, below the 4 to 6 percent international benchmark, and spending is often concentrated in areas that do not generate strong learning gains.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Efficiency of spend, not just quantum, is the reform lever.
insights.locator: At the same time, these learning gaps persist

insights.claim: A World Bank Group paper estimates demographic change alone could free fiscal space by 2050 of about 0.53 percentage points of GDP for primary education and 0.47 points for secondary education relative to 2020.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Freed fiscal space could be redirected to quality improvements or other budget priorities.
insights.locator: A new World Bank Group paper

insights.claim: Even with an ambitious expansion toward universal pre-primary, primary and secondary enrollment, demographic change could leave room to raise per-student spending toward high-income country levels by 2050.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Rising per-student spend implies growing quality-focused education markets despite fewer students.
insights.locator: Even after accounting for an ambitious expansion

insights.claim: Falling student numbers do not automatically cut costs because fixed expenses such as buildings, administration and transport do not shrink on their own; without reform per-student costs rise while learning stays weak.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Demographic dividend in education is conditional on active consolidation.
insights.quote: Falling student numbers do not necessarily reduce costs
insights.locator: In countries with shrinking school-age populations

insights.claim: Bhutan and the Maldives may finance higher per-student spending largely from demographic gains, while Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are likely to need additional resources to reach ambitious quality targets.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Differentiated fiscal pressure: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka face larger education spending needs.
insights.locator: Bhutan and the Maldives, for example

insights.claim: India stands out as a country where demographic change could create meaningful room for education reinvestment, while Nepal's outcome depends on enrollment patterns and system efficiency.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: India's education budget may gain fiscal headroom from demographics.

insights.claim: Countries in Europe and Central Asia with declining student populations did not automatically realise savings because school system structure stayed unchanged, locking in inefficiency.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests South Asia's dividend will be partly squandered absent reform.
insights.quote: demographic change creates an opportunity—but only if governments act before inefficiencies become locked in
insights.locator: International experience offers an important cautionary lesson

insights.claim: School consolidation can improve efficiency and quality but is politically sensitive, requiring transparent communication, community engagement, safe student transport and upgraded receiving schools.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Consolidation creates demand for student transport and school facility upgrades.
insights.quote: Schools are community institutions, not just budget lines.
insights.locator: Second, plan the structure of the school system early

insights.claim: Governments should protect education budgets and reinvest demographic savings in evidence-backed areas such as improved pedagogy, structured teaching support and teaching at the right level.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Structured-pedagogy and TaRL providers are positioned to benefit from reinvested budgets.
